title: Spin Awareness & Recovery

required_knowledge_points.title: Spin Aerodynamics — Autorotation and the Asymmetric Stall
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'What is a spin and what two conditions must exist for one to occur?' A spin requires TWO things simultaneously: (1) the wing must be stalled (exceeding critical AOA), AND (2) the aircraft must be yawing (uncoordinated). Both wings are stalled — but one is MORE stalled than the other. This asymmetry drives the autorotation.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: A SPIN is an aggravated stall resulting in autorotation — a self-sustaining rotation driven by asymmetric lift and drag on stalled lifting surfaces. TWO PREREQUISITES: (1) Both wings stalled (AOA above critical). (2) Yawing moment (uncoordinated flight). AUTOROTATION PHYSICS: when the aircraft stalls while yawing (e.g., left rudder), the left wing drops and retreats. The relative wind strikes the dropping left wing from below, INCREASING its AOA — pushing it DEEPER into the stall. The right wing rises, and the relative wind strikes it from above, DECREASING its AOA — pushing it CLOSER to (or slightly below) the critical AOA. Result: left wing = deep stall = less lift + MORE drag. Right wing = shallow stall = more lift + LESS drag. This asymmetry creates a self-reinforcing loop: the right wing generates more lift (rolling left) and less drag (allowing the nose to yaw further left). The aircraft is locked into autorotation. THE 'ONE WING FLYING' MYTH: BOTH wings are stalled. One is simply MORE stalled than the other. SPIN vs. SPIRAL DIVE: in a spin, wings are stalled and airspeed is LOW and stable. In a spiral dive, wings are NOT stalled and airspeed is HIGH and increasing rapidly toward Vne. CERTIFICATION: Normal category = tested for 1-turn inadvertent spin + 1-turn recovery only. NOT approved for intentional spins. Utility/Acrobatic = tested for up to 6-turn spins, approved for intentional spins within W&B limits. FLAT SPIN: if a Normal category aircraft enters a multi-turn spin, the nose may rise toward the horizon (spin flattens). The rudder and elevator can become blanked by the fuselage/wing wake — making recovery IMPOSSIBLE. PARACHUTE RULE (91.307): intentional maneuvers exceeding 60° bank or 30° pitch require parachutes. Exception: spins given by a CFI for certificate training.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Two Prerequisites for a Spin
```
1. Wings STALLED (both wings above critical AOA)
   +
2. YAWING moment (uncoordinated flight — rudder input, P-factor, adverse yaw)
   =
   SPIN (autorotation)
```

### Autorotation — The Self-Reinforcing Loop
| Wing | Movement | Effect on AOA | Stall Depth | Lift | Drag |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Inside** (dropping) | Retreating | AOA **increases** | Deeper stall | ↓ Less | ↑ More |
| **Outside** (rising) | Advancing | AOA **decreases** | Shallower stall | ↑ More | ↓ Less |

Result: asymmetric lift rolls the aircraft INTO the spin; asymmetric drag yaws it INTO the spin → **self-sustaining**

### Spin vs. Spiral Dive
| Parameter | Spin | Spiral Dive |
|---|---|---|
| Wings | **STALLED** | NOT stalled |
| Airspeed | LOW, stable | **HIGH, increasing** toward Vne |
| Recovery | PARE (reduce AOA, stop yaw) | Reduce power, level wings |

### Aircraft Category Limits
| Category | Spin Approval | Testing |
|---|---|---|
| **Normal** | ❌ NOT approved for intentional spins | 1-turn + 1-turn recovery only |
| **Utility** | ✅ Approved (within W&B limits) | Up to 6 turns |
| **Acrobatic** | ✅ Approved | Extended spins |

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'Are both wings stalled in a spin?' YES. Both are stalled. One is just MORE stalled than the other. The myth that 'one wing is flying' is false.

required_knowledge_points.title: Spin Phases — Entry, Incipient, Developed, and Recovery
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'Describe the four phases of a spin.' The incipient phase (first 1-2 turns) is the golden window for recovery — the autorotation hasn't locked in yet, and neutralizing controls may be sufficient. Once the spin develops (steady-state rotation), you need the full PARE procedure, and altitude loss accelerates to 4,000-6,000 fpm.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: A spin progresses through four sequential aerodynamic phases (AC 61-67C). PHASE 1 — ENTRY: the pilot exceeds the critical AOA while the aircraft is yawing. Pro-spin inputs are present: stall + rudder. This is the PREVENTABLE phase — if the pilot recognizes impending stall and coordinates, no spin occurs. PHASE 2 — INCIPIENT (1-2 turns): the transitional chaos phase. Rotation begins and accelerates. Aerodynamic forces (lift/drag) and inertial forces (centrifugal/gyroscopic) are fighting for dominance. Pitch attitude, rotation rate, and flight path are erratic and changing rapidly. This is the OPTIMAL recovery window: the autorotation is not yet locked in. Simply neutralizing the controls (releasing rudder/elevator pressure) will often stop the rotation. PHASE 3 — DEVELOPED (steady state): the spin matures. Aerodynamic and inertial forces are perfectly balanced. Rotation rate, pitch attitude, and vertical speed are STABILIZED from turn to turn. Vertical descent rate: typically 4,000-6,000 fpm. Indicated airspeed: LOW and stable (near published stall speed — NOT increasing). The massive drag of the stalled wings acts like a parachute, preventing acceleration. Recovery now requires the full PARE procedure with deliberate, full-deflection inputs. PHASE 4 — RECOVERY: begins when proper anti-spin inputs are applied and ends when the aircraft returns to normal, unstalled, level flight. Duration depends on aircraft design, CG position, and how deeply developed the spin became. Can take 0.5 to several turns. ALTITUDE LOSS: approximately 500 feet per turn in the incipient/developed phase. A spin entered at 800 ft AGL in the traffic pattern is UNRECOVERABLE — there is not enough altitude for the recovery pull-out.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### The Four Phases of a Spin
| Phase | Duration | What Happens | Pilot Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Entry** | Pre-stall | Stall + yaw = spin begins | **PREVENT:** coordinate, reduce AOA |
| **2. Incipient** | 1-2 turns | Chaotic, rotation accelerating | **RECOVER NOW:** neutralize controls or PARE |
| **3. Developed** | Steady-state | Balanced forces, stabilized rotation | **PARE procedure** with full-deflection inputs |
| **4. Recovery** | 0.5-2+ turns | Anti-spin inputs breaking autorotation | Neutralize rudder after rotation stops, smooth pull-out |

### Key Metrics
- **Altitude loss:** ~500 ft per turn
- **Vertical speed (developed):** 4,000-6,000 fpm descent
- **Indicated airspeed:** LOW and stable (near Vs, NOT increasing)
- **Incipient phase duration:** 2-4 seconds (first 1-2 turns)

### Why the Incipient Phase Is the Golden Window
- Autorotation NOT yet locked in
- Simply **neutralizing controls** often stops rotation
- Altitude loss is minimal (1-2 turns = ~500-1,000 ft)
- Once DEVELOPED → requires full PARE + more altitude

### The Traffic Pattern Death Trap
```
Spin entry at 800 ft AGL → 500 ft/turn altitude loss
→ 1.5 turns to recognize + apply PARE = 750 ft lost
→ Recovery dive pull-out = additional 200-500 ft
→ Total needed: ~1,000-1,500 ft minimum
→ 800 ft available → UNRECOVERABLE
```

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'When is the best time to recover from a spin?' INCIPIENT PHASE. Not developed. The earlier you act, the less altitude you lose.

required_knowledge_points.title: Spin Recovery — The PARE Procedure
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'What is the PARE recovery procedure and why does each step work?' PARE is a sequenced algorithm — Power idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder full opposite, Elevator forward. Each step systematically dismantles the autorotation. Get the order wrong and you deepen the spin. And after recovery, if you hold the opposite rudder too long, you snap into a CROSSOVER spin in the other direction.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: PARE is the NASA standard spin recovery procedure. Each step serves a specific aerodynamic function. P — POWER TO IDLE: in a spin, power is the ENEMY. The propeller slipstream increases airflow over the horizontal stabilizer, pushing the tail DOWN and the nose UP — FLATTENING the spin. A flat spin blanks the rudder (fuselage/wing wake blocks airflow), making recovery impossible. Propeller gyroscopic precession can also accelerate the spin rate. Cutting power removes ALL pro-spin propeller effects. A — AILERONS NEUTRAL: the untrained reflex is to 'roll out' with ailerons. This is FATAL. If spinning left, right aileron deflects the LEFT aileron DOWN — INCREASING the AOA on the already deeply stalled left wing. This deepens the stall on the pro-spin wing, accelerating autorotation. Ailerons MUST be neutral. R — RUDDER FULL OPPOSITE: the rudder creates anti-spin yawing torque. Full deflection is required — partial or timid rudder will not break a developed spin. For a left spin, apply FULL RIGHT rudder. E — ELEVATOR BRISKLY FORWARD: after yaw is arrested, both wings are STILL STALLED. Pushing the elevator forward (to neutral or slightly past) reduces pitch attitude, decreasing the AOA below the critical threshold. This breaks the stall, reattaching the boundary layer to both wings. THE PULL-OUT: after PARE, rotation stops. IMMEDIATELY neutralize the rudder — holding opposite rudder after rotation stops will snap the aircraft into a CROSSOVER SPIN in the opposite direction. Then SMOOTHLY pull out of the dive. Too aggressive = secondary stall → back into the spin. ALWAYS follow POH first if it differs from PARE (some aircraft require immediate flap retraction or specific elevator timing).
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### PARE — Step by Step
| Step | Input | Aerodynamic Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **P** | Power to **IDLE** | Remove propeller effects: slipstream flattens spin, precession accelerates rotation |
| **A** | Ailerons **NEUTRAL** | Prevent deepening the stall on the pro-spin wing via aileron AOA increase |
| **R** | Rudder **FULL OPPOSITE** | Create anti-spin yawing torque to break autorotation |
| **E** | Elevator **BRISKLY FORWARD** | Reduce AOA below critical → break the stall on both wings |

### After PARE — The Pull-Out
```
1. Rotation stops → IMMEDIATELY neutralize rudder
   (Holding opposite rudder → CROSSOVER SPIN in other direction)
2. Smoothly pull out of the dive
   (Too aggressive → SECONDARY STALL → back into spin)
3. Add power to arrest altitude loss
4. Return to level flight
```

### Why Each Error Is Fatal
| Error | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Using ailerons to 'roll out' | Deepens stall on pro-spin wing → accelerates spin |
| Timid/partial rudder | Insufficient torque to break developed autorotation |
| Power NOT at idle | Slipstream flattens spin → rudder blanking → unrecoverable |
| Holding opposite rudder too long | **Crossover spin** in opposite direction |
| Aggressive pull-out | Secondary stall → re-entry into spin |

### POH Is Final Authority
- PARE is the universal standard
- Some POHs add: retract flaps immediately, specific elevator timing
- **Always follow the POH** if it differs from generic PARE

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'What is the most common fatal error in spin recovery?' Using ailerons. The pilot's reflex is to turn the yoke — but this increases AOA on the stalled wing and accelerates the autorotation.

lesson_overview:
## Spin Awareness — The Aerodynamics of Autorotation and the PARE Recovery

This lesson covers the theory, recognition, and recovery procedure for spins — the most violent outcome of a mishandled stall. While private pilots are not required to perform actual spins on the checkride, understanding spin aerodynamics is essential because spins kill more GA pilots than any other loss-of-control event.

**A spin requires two simultaneous conditions: both wings stalled and a yawing moment.** Neither condition alone produces a spin. A coordinated stall produces a straight nose-drop. Uncoordinated flight without a stall produces a skid or slip. But when the wing exceeds the critical AOA while the aircraft is yawing — from rudder input, P-factor, or adverse yaw — the result is autorotation. The dropping wing retreats through the airmass, increasing its local AOA and deepening its stall. The rising wing advances, decreasing its AOA and generating more lift. This asymmetry is self-reinforcing: the lift differential rolls the aircraft into the spin, and the drag differential yaws it further, maintaining the rotation indefinitely. Both wings are stalled — the myth that 'one wing is flying' is aerodynamically incorrect.

**A spin progresses through four distinct phases, each with different recovery characteristics.** The entry phase is where the pilot provides the pro-spin inputs — stall plus yaw. The incipient phase spans the first one to two turns, during which the aerodynamic and inertial forces are still fighting for dominance. This is the golden window: the autorotation is not yet locked in, and simply neutralizing the controls often stops the rotation. The developed phase represents steady-state autorotation — rotation rate, pitch attitude, and descent rate are all stabilized, with vertical descent rates of 4,000 to 6,000 feet per minute. The recovery phase begins when proper anti-spin inputs are applied and ends when the aircraft returns to normal flight. At pattern altitude — 500 to 800 feet AGL — a spin is mathematically unrecoverable before ground impact.

**The PARE procedure is a sequenced algorithm that systematically dismantles the autorotation.** Power to idle removes the propeller slipstream that flattens the spin and blocks the rudder. Ailerons neutral prevents the pilot's instinctive roll input from deepening the stall on the pro-spin wing. Full opposite rudder creates the anti-spin yawing torque that breaks the rotation. Elevator briskly forward reduces the AOA below the critical threshold, breaking the stall on both wings simultaneously. After recovery, the pilot must immediately neutralize the rudder — holding opposite rudder after the rotation stops will snap the aircraft into a crossover spin in the opposite direction. The dive pull-out must be smooth and gentle to avoid a secondary stall. And the aircraft's POH is always the final authority — some designs require specific modifications to the generic PARE sequence.
